utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday at page 7151, line 21, beginning at line 21, you were asked a series of questions and gave these answers, and this is beginning with: "Q. But then the question was whether you have knowledge of the propelling charge that was used for the projectile that landed near the entrance of the Markale market. And you responded: "The angle of impact enables specialists who are familiar with the firing tables of this piece of artillery to determine that they are in the presence either of a maximum charge, charge 6, six packets of propelling powder placed under the projectile of the propellant; or a charge 1, one packet of powder placed under the shell. There are -- only these two cases are possible and only -- it's either a minimum charge 1 or a maximum charge 6 which provides a proper explanation." Then another question, the follow-up question: "Do you consider yourself to have specialist knowledge on these matters or are you referring to specialists other than you, you being unable to verify whether it's accurate what they told you?" And you responded: "I have basic knowledge on mortar firing like any officer, but firing tables were used by true specialists, i.e., the team of investigators at the engineering unit, and this is what they specified in their report." And that report you've now told you us is what we see on the screen at 102 -- 65 ter 10243, which remains on the screen. So I'd like to go back to that specific set of questions and answers. And I would ask you, you would agree, would you not, that 10243 does not contain any recorded information about the two possible charges, minimum charge 1 or maximum charge 6, which you testified about yesterday in that selection of testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us to the best of your recollection how that information was relayed to you?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would assume that your question deals with the maximum and minimum charges. My answer is the following. We had within our military staff and within the forces specialists in artillery who went into analysis of these results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's not the question, Witness. The question was: From where did you receive the information that it should have been propelling charge, either 1 or 6, thus, excluding, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Where that is found, where that was -- how this was conveyed to you. Ms. Hochhauser, that was the question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still not an answer to the question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: How this information, which is not found in the report, was conveyed to you. Not who formed that opinion or who reached that conclusion, but how you received this information which is not found in this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a military staff work around the table in an operational centre with all the specialists gathered, and they talked, they confront their analysis in order to get to a conclusion that would be collectively adopted by all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still not an answer to the question. Unfortunately, Ms. Hochhauser, I leave it your hands whether you want to pursue the matter or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us, was it, to the best of your recollection, relayed to you orally or in writing, that information, if you have a recollection information? The information about charge 1 or charge 6, was it conveyed to by word or by -- in writing?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the result of an analysis that was done in an operational -- operation room by different officers who knew their job, and they were comparing their viewpoint and reached this conclusion, conclusion that I took in charge myself at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, were you present in that room when they reached that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. These surveys were done in the operation rooming of Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the time, yes. And in this specific case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it was conveyed to you -- you heard them discussing it, and you heard them reaching this conclusion. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I gathered these individuals. We analysed the conclusions. We compared, as I said earlier, compared them with the data coming from the radar personnel. We saw all these observations, and this enabled me to structure these solutions that I have offered.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, what was your understanding of which warring party held the territory that corresponded with the firing positions for this shell if the propellant charge was the minimum charge 1 and if it was the minimum [sic] charge 6?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our understanding was that with -- in the hypothesis of the maximum charge 6, the shot came from a region that was located on the north side, north-east of the Mount Trebevic, which was controlled by the SRK. In the hypothesis of a minimum charge 1, the distance that was about 1.000 metres would match a zone that was held by the SRK in proximity to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: If we can turn back into private session and then I'm reaching -- it's my last subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one additional question of this matter. This is a very relevant conclusion. Do you have any explanation why it's not presented in the report or do you have any knowledge of these conclusions being presented in other reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I neglected to also offer that document into evidence. The engineering report. 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Sorry, 10243.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our opinion is that this document is too technical to be introduced through this witness because we have to know more about the background, so we think that the people who are more trained in ballistics would be better to have this document introduced through. So we would object to having this document introduced through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hochhauser.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the witness has commented on it and it's an associated exhibit to his -- to his statement. If the Court were inclined to agree with Mr. Lukic, I would say -- I would request that it be entered as a bar table document, since it is closely associated with this witness and there will be other people who will need it during the course of their testimony, including the experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, isn't it true that you relied on the report for the 68 degrees?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, 67, 68. Now if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I got it from the witness that he knows that it was 67.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I leave it with Your Honours to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then the document can be admitted. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10243 receives number P755, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P755 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Actually, if we could briefly have 10239 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much more time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I would say about seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Seven minutes. Then perhaps it would make sense to have that seven minutes before the next break. I'm also looking at you, Mr. Lukic, and Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no problem with having this [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless I hear otherwise you may proceed, Ms. Hochhauser. Yes. Mr. Mladic would prefer to have a break, I take it. I didn't invite for consultations. Break or no break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It appears that Mr. Mladic needs a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break. We'll first move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Hochhauser, you have got until five minutes until 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, if we could continue in private session. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Further cross-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, although I had promised that those were all the questions I had for you, I have just one or two more and then we're done. You know what this document is. It's a report of the sniper battalion on the 20th of September 1994. You were not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need page 2 in B/C/S. We also need page 2 in French. Actually, in English, it's also the second page, because we have on our screens the English and French versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said page 2 in French as well, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the second page in French as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the second page in French, only it's obviously the third one in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move, for the English, to the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's a reference is to the commander of the 2nd Battalion. In French, I see that it's the second paragraph; and in English it is the third paragraph. It says: "The commander of the 2nd Battalion accepted the report drawn up and presented by the commanding officer. Even though he was surprised and furious at having been given it, he promised to investigate the matter thoroughly. He looked sincere and truly annoyed by an operation which he had clearly overlooked and which he had not ordered." There's a reference here to the commander of the 2nd Battalion. It's Mr. Petrovic, isn't it, commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right? We see that from this document. Although in French, it's on the previous page. In the English version, it's at the top of the page. You see the last paragraph down there, the last paragraph in the French version. So is this the commander of the 2nd Battalion that is being referred to?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading as you do that, indeed, it is Mr. Petrovic who is the commander of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it customary to talk to the Serb side about sniping incidents as they were happening?

utterances.speaker: RM055 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such was the process that was implemented at the beginning of 1994. This procedure seems, for what I learned of it, to have been approximately implemented in 1994 until November. Date at which things went downhill and the circuits that were implemented and approved by the warring parties did not work anymore, and this type of contact from May, the date at which I was on duty in Sarajevo, these mechanisms did not work anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need one clarification while the witness is here, Your Honour. Regarding this video, 22421, when the Prosecution proposed that somebody was telling, "It's not correct, it's not correct," is it clear now that it has nothing to do with the measurement done by the French soldier? That's how I understood Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the way in which I described it is that -- whether it had anything to do with that, I would not know on the basis of this video. The only thing I can establish is that the words were spoken well prior to what seems to be the -- the -- the measurement itself, although some beginning was made to the extent that it seems that he had the compass in his hands or something like that. But before he kneels down close to the crater and starts manipulating the compass, it's well before that moment that the words were spoken. That is the factual observations I made in describing this. I'm not saying that it was not linked to it. I can't see that on the video --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, we stipulated it. But the Prosecution didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOCHHAUSER
utterances.text: I think I was nodding my ascent. Yes, those words were spoken before -- on the video clearly before he is kneeling down to take the measurement and pronounces the degrees read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I have no further questions for the witness, although I might have a few matters to be raised in relation to his testimony. But, at this movement, I have no further questions to the witness. Neither have my colleagues. [Interpretation] Which means, sir, that this will conclude your deposition and I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Chamber, and I wish you a -- I wish you a good return home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into closed session. Yes, and, of course, the same wishes extends to the representative of the French government.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I would like to make a few observations. As far as the Markale, the second Markale incident is concerned, of course, we have received the evidence of this witness, stating that it should have been charges 1 and/or 6. The Chamber, to the extent there exists any evidence which would further -- would shed further light on these issues which are of a highly technical nature where the witness was unable to give as much, the Chamber would appreciate if that, not necessarily immediately but sooner or later, would become part of the record so that we are better able to assess the testimony of the present witness. That is one. And then I have another matter which I do not express on behalf of the Chamber. Mr. Lukic, you have put a question to this witness. I'm referring you to page 36, line 14. You said -- and the witness was unable to answer the question. But you said, when you were referring to the statement made by - let me see or was it, Colonel Lugonja - in the question preceding the answer, you said: "The Serbs understood the withdrawal or collection of weapons as follows. If they are attacked, they have the right to use those weapons. So these are the same rights that envisaged by the protocol that we are looking at a moment ago." Now the witness said that he remembered that those words were spoken. What I'd like to draw your attention to is the following, that in the protocol in paragraph 1, the wording is different. The first section of paragraph 1 dealing with the situation that UNPROFOR withdraws for any reason from mutually agreed sites for the regrouping of heavy weapons without the agreement of the BSA, or that it withdraws from its interposition areas between the Serb and Muslim lines, there it is claimed by the BSA, or at least they reserve their right, to redeploy these weapons. However, for the second situation, which is about attacks, the language is different. The language says that, If there are attacks that cannot be immediately stopped, that the BSA reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence. I'm pointing at this because in the way in which you put it to the witness, you were talking about the use of weapons, which seems to be a reference to the redeployment of the weapons, but you linked that to attacks and not to the withdrawal of UNPROFOR. I just wanted -- and there was no need to put it again to the witness in view of his answer, but I just want to draw your attention that there are two different situations described in the protocol with approximately two different -- not necessarily excluding one from another, but two different possible consequences for which the Serb forces reserved their right. I -- I just -- I'm making this observation in order to avoid any confusion in the future about this protocol. At the same time, we have dealt with the protocol in quite some detail in December. We have dealt with the protocol now again, and it was in all circumstances we are still troubled by what the exact status was. If there would be any documentary evidence from February 1994 which would shed further light on what way this protocol went, whether it was approved or not, whether there are any signed copies, signed by whom, that certainly would assist the Chamber in evaluating the evidence we heard today and on the 12th of December. Having said this -- yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two matters to raise if we can make use of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's not much time. You mean those 40 seconds remaining, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, from here it looks like I have two minutes but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Sometimes the view of the Chamber is different from the view of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with respect to scheduling I -- I as well was concerned about the schedule for this week and spoke with General Smith. He is available to work as late as the Chamber wishes on Thursday evening. He is unable Friday evening. And is able to come back Monday although, it would create some problems, but he would able to return Monday if we were unable to finish. I can commit the Prosecution to our two hours. If Mr. Ivetic still believes can he do it in - and I think six hours is what he estimated, that would require a single hour extra tomorrow, and the Prosecution would certainly appreciate the Chamber considering whether to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber certainly will consider it but preferably on the basis of a well-agreed schedule by the parties. Now you could say this is the two hours and the six hours explain everything, but we would rather have it in sessions because sometimes some minutes are not stolen from the parties but sometimes are used by the Chamber to allow the parties to move on more quickly as they would have done without the Chamber's assistance. Now, so, therefore, a firm commitment of the parties would certainly encourage the Chamber to agree to that. Any other matter, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is one other important matter, Your Honour. I'd ask that we go into private session for me to raise this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First of all, I'd like to apologise to all those assisting us for our late finish. Second, I invite Mr. Lukic to liaise with the Registry about the possibility of an extended session so that the Registrar will inform the Chamber, and I'd like to ask the Registrar already to prepare or to anticipate for an extended session tomorrow for, I would say, for one or two hours. You never know how things happen. We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 24th of January, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
